title: Bachmann, Landau, and the Origin of Big-O Notation
explainer: Big-O notation didn't start in computer science: the German mathematician Paul Bachmann introduced the 'O' notation in 1894 to describe growth rates in number theory, and Edmund Landau popularized and put it on a formal footing in 1909 (which is why it's sometimes called a 'Landau symbol'). Computer scientists borrowed this decades-old mathematical notation wholesale in the 1960s-70s to describe algorithm running time rather than inventing a new one. It's a useful reminder that the 'shape' of growth rates was a mathematical concern long before computers existed to run the algorithms.

title: Cobham's Thesis: Defining 'Efficient' Before It Could Be Tested
explainer: In the mid-1960s, Alan Cobham and (independently) Jack Edmonds proposed what's now called the Cobham-Edmonds thesis: that a problem should count as 'efficiently' or 'feasibly' solvable only if some algorithm solves it in polynomial time. That was a deliberate definitional choice, not a discovered law, and it's exactly the line a complexity-analysis class draws when it treats O(n^2) as 'fine' and O(2^n) as 'intractable.' It's also the historical seed that later grew into the P vs NP question.
